Meaning of Indo-Saracenic architecture

Indo-Saracenic architecture developed as an important architectural approach during the British colonial period. It combined elements taken from Indian architectural traditions with European approaches to the planning and construction of large buildings.

The historical term Indo-Saracenic reflects colonial-era European terminology. Saracenic was historically used by Europeans in reference to Muslim or Islamic cultures. However, the buildings classified as Indo-Saracenic in India drew upon more than one Indian tradition, including elements associated with Hindu, Jain, Sultanate and Mughal architecture.

Indo-Saracenic architecture should not be treated as identical to the earlier Indo-Islamic architecture of medieval India. The latter developed under Indian Sultanates, the Mughals and other regional patrons. Indo-Saracenic architecture, as examined in the colonial context, is a later approach that reused and combined selected Indian forms in buildings designed for colonial authorities, princely states and other patrons.

Principal architectural features

  • Domes: Rounded roof structures, often placed above important halls, entrances or central spaces.
  • Chhatris: Small domed pavilions, commonly supported by columns. They were prominent in several Indian architectural traditions.
  • Jalis: Perforated screens, often using geometrical or ornamental patterns. They can admit filtered light and air while reducing direct exposure.
  • Arches: Entrances and openings using curved or pointed forms inspired by different architectural traditions.
  • Indian decorative motifs: Details drawn from regional architecture, including carved brackets, ornamental patterns and other recognisable forms.
  • European planning and construction approaches: Organised spaces suited to the functions of institutions, palaces, courts or other large buildings.

Not every Indo-Saracenic building includes every feature. The central idea is the deliberate combination of architectural traditions within one design.

Important examples outside Gujarat

Gateway of India, Mumbai

The Gateway of India is a major Indo-Saracenic monument at Apollo Bunder in Mumbai. It was intended to commemorate the visit of King George V and Queen Mary in 1911.

The architect was George Wittet. The foundation stone was laid on 31 March 1911, the final design was sanctioned in 1914, and the monument was completed in 1924.

These dates must be distinguished carefully. The event commemorated by the monument occurred in 1911, but the permanent monument was not completed until 1924.

Other examples

The Madras High Court in Chennai and the historic Taj Mahal Palace Hotel in Mumbai are important examples associated with Indo-Saracenic architecture. They demonstrate the use of Indian architectural forms in buildings serving very different functions.

Lakshmi Vilas Palace, Vadodara

Lakshmi Vilas Palace, also written as Laxmi Vilas Palace or Lukshmi Vilas Palace, is one of Gujarat's most important examples of Indo-Saracenic architecture. It was built under the patronage of Maharaja Sayajirao Gaekwad III of Baroda and completed in 1890.

The palace combines an impressive monumental appearance with architectural features derived from different Indian and European traditions. Its design reflects the ambitions and resources of the princely state of Baroda during the colonial period.

Architects of Lakshmi Vilas Palace

The palace was originally designed by Major Charles Mant. After Mant's death in 1881, the project was completed by Robert Fellowes Chisholm.

These are different contributions to the same building. Mant was the original designer, while Chisholm carried forward and completed the project. An examination statement attributing the original design exclusively to Chisholm would therefore be inaccurate.

Baroda College and the Faculty of Arts

Baroda College was established in 1881. The historic main building, now associated with the Faculty of Arts of the Maharaja Sayajirao University of Baroda, was designed by Robert Fellowes Chisholm in the Indo-Saracenic style.

Its design includes Indian and Byzantine-influenced arches and domes. The principal dome of its convocation hall was modelled on the great dome of Gol Gumbaz at Bijapur.

This provides an important example of architectural inspiration moving from an earlier Indian monument to a later colonial-period institutional building. The establishment of Baroda College in 1881 must also be distinguished from the establishment of the Maharaja Sayajirao University of Baroda in 1949.

Important building and architect associations

BuildingPlacePrincipal association
Gateway of IndiaMumbaiGeorge Wittet; completed 1924
Lakshmi Vilas PalaceVadodaraCharles Mant; completed by Robert Fellowes Chisholm; 1890
Historic Baroda College main buildingVadodaraRobert Fellowes Chisholm; Indo-Saracenic
Madras High CourtChennaiImportant Indo-Saracenic public building
Taj Mahal Palace HotelMumbaiImportant Indo-Saracenic hotel building

Prelims focus

  • Indo-Saracenic architecture combines Indian architectural forms with European approaches to building design.
  • Typical elements include domes, chhatris, jalis and arches.
  • George Wittet designed the Gateway of India; its permanent structure was completed in 1924.
  • Lakshmi Vilas Palace, Vadodara, was completed in 1890.
  • Charles Mant originally designed Lakshmi Vilas Palace; Robert Fellowes Chisholm completed it.
  • Trap: Baroda College was established in 1881, while the Maharaja Sayajirao University of Baroda was established in 1949.

[NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part III, Class 12, Theme 12, Colonial Cities, printed pp. 342–343, 2019–2020 reprint; Mumbai City District Administration, Gateway of India, History and architectural description; Gujarat Tourism, Lukshmi Vilas Palace, About the Location and Brief History; British Library, Photo 2/7(9), Laxmi Vilas Palace, Baroda, catalogue description; Maharaja Sayajirao University of Baroda, Origin and History and Faculty of Arts, About Faculty; online sources consulted 23 November 2026.]

title: Indo-Saracenic Architecture: Hybrid Forms and Important Buildings in Gujarat

body:
Meaning of town planning

Town planning concerns the organisation and development of settlements. It includes the location and arrangement of roads, public buildings, commercial areas, residential neighbourhoods, military facilities, open spaces and other urban functions.

A building's architectural style and a city's plan answer different questions. The style identifies the building's principal design characteristics. Town planning explains how buildings and other urban spaces are arranged in relation to one another.

Growth of colonial port cities

Madras, Bombay and Calcutta became major centres of commerce and administration under British rule. Trading settlements expanded as the East India Company's commercial and political influence increased. Harbours, warehouses, offices, military establishments and residential districts developed around the growing centres.

The cities did not develop according to one identical master plan. Their particular geography, earlier settlements, trading functions and political circumstances influenced their growth. Nevertheless, several important patterns can be recognised across colonial urban development.

Forts and commercial centres

Early British trading settlements were frequently organised around fortified areas. Fortifications protected commercial interests and military establishments, while roads and marketplaces connected the ports to the wider settlement.

Fort St George at Madras and Fort William at Calcutta were important colonial fortifications. Bombay also developed as a major fortified trading and administrative centre.

White Town and Black Town

In several colonial settlements, European residential and institutional areas became known as White Town, while areas largely inhabited by Indian merchants, artisans, workers and other residents were called Black Town.

These were historical labels reflecting racial and social divisions under colonial rule. They do not refer to the colours of buildings. Their boundaries and characteristics also changed with the expansion of the cities.

The distinction illustrates how the organisation of urban space could reinforce inequalities. Access to accommodation, amenities and important institutions was influenced by the structure of colonial society.

Civil Lines, cantonments and bungalows

Civil Lines

Civil Lines were areas associated particularly with European officials and their residences. They often contained broad roads, large residential plots, gardens and buildings separated from densely populated older neighbourhoods.

Cantonments

A cantonment was an area developed mainly for the stationing and administration of military forces. Its facilities could include barracks, parade grounds, offices and associated residential accommodation.

The distinction is functional: Civil Lines were principally connected with civilian officials and their residences, while cantonments were principally connected with the military.

The colonial bungalow

The bungalow became an important residential form during the colonial period. It commonly had a relatively low structure, a pitched roof, a verandah and open space around the building.

The verandah was especially useful in the Indian climate because it provided a shaded transitional space between the exterior and the main rooms. Colonial bungalows therefore illustrate the adaptation of residential architecture to local conditions.

Surveys, roads and sanitation

Colonial governments prepared maps and collected information about roads, buildings, settlement patterns and urban conditions. Such information was used to organise trade, taxation, administration and public works.

Road construction, drainage, water supply and sanitation became increasingly important concerns as colonial cities grew. Planning interventions were not always socially neutral: some improvements benefited particular areas while poorer settlements faced displacement, stricter controls or inadequate services.

Therefore, colonial town planning must be understood as both a physical activity and an expression of administrative priorities.

New Delhi: a planned imperial capital

On 12 December 1911, the decision to transfer the capital of British India from Calcutta to Delhi was announced at the Delhi Durbar.

A new administrative capital was subsequently planned in the area around Raisina Hill. The principal architects and planners associated with New Delhi were Edwin Lutyens and Herbert Baker.

The plan emphasised broad avenues, formal relationships between important buildings, gardens, open spaces and ceremonial approaches. Such arrangements expressed the power and prestige of the colonial government.

Important buildings and designers

  • Viceroy's House, now Rashtrapati Bhavan: Designed by Edwin Lutyens. The building combines European classical planning with Indian architectural elements, including its prominent dome, chhatris and jalis.
  • North Block and South Block: The major Secretariat buildings were designed by Herbert Baker.
  • India Gate: A prominent ceremonial monument associated with the planned imperial capital.

The central dome of Rashtrapati Bhavan is particularly associated with inspiration from the Great Stupa at Sanchi. This is an important example of Indian architectural influence within a colonial administrative building.

New Delhi was officially opened as the imperial capital on 15 February 1931. This date is distinct from the announcement of the capital transfer in 1911.

How colonial planning differs from later modern planning

Colonial urban layouts frequently reflected the needs of trade, defence, imperial administration and social separation. The planning of New Delhi placed particular emphasis on ceremonial authority and monumental government buildings.

Post-Independence planned cities such as Chandigarh and Gandhinagar placed greater emphasis on organised residential sectors, public institutions, transport connections and open spaces intended to serve the functions of a modern capital. The transition was not absolute, since roads, gardens and regular layouts were also important in colonial plans.

Prelims focus

  • Important colonial port cities included Madras, Bombay and Calcutta.
  • White Town and Black Town were historical terms associated with racial and social separation.
  • Civil Lines were associated with civilian officials; cantonments were associated with military establishments.
  • The transfer of the British Indian capital from Calcutta to Delhi was announced on 12 December 1911.
  • Edwin Lutyens designed Viceroy's House; Herbert Baker designed the North and South Secretariat Blocks.
  • Trap: The capital-transfer announcement occurred in 1911, but New Delhi was officially opened in 1931.

[NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part III, Class 12, Theme 12, Colonial Cities, printed pp. 320–328 and 338–340, 2019–2020 reprint; New Delhi Municipal Council, History, capital-transfer decision and official opening; Rashtrapati Bhavan, The President's Secretariat and Making of Rashtrapati Bhavan, architectural design and Indian elements; Delhi Tourism, New Delhi, historical description; official websites consulted 23 November 2026.]

title: Colonial Town Planning: Port Cities, Civil Lines and New Delhi
